articles.text: About a dozen members of the Piedmont Garden Club and Beautification Foundation woke up early yesterday to string festive lights on the 80-foot tall redwood tree in front of the Community Hall. Public Works employees began installing strands of colored lights on the tree starting at 9 a.m. Tuesday, December 1, using a hydraulic boom lift. The Beautification Foundation took over the preparations for the ceremony more than 50 years ago, in the mid-1960s. The labor-intensive process begins with volunteers checking each bulb to ensure they are untangled and working. Unwound, the lights cover the entirety of the Community Hall floor, and are then carried strand by strand to the base of the tree, where they are raised to the top by a cherry picker. This year, volunteers observed social distancing and each person donned a mask. Traditionally, a large crowd gathers for a nighttime celebration when the lights are first turned on. A virtual tree lighting will be observed tonight, Wednesday, December 2, at 7 p.m. on KCOM, Piedmont Channel 27. A tree-lighting ceremony was taped last night, December 1, with speeches by Mayor Bob McBain, City Administrator Sara Lillevand, Piedmont Beautification Foundation president Gayle Lambert, and former foundation president Patty Siskind. Music will be performed by the Piedmont High School Troubadours. Residents are asked not to gather in person for this year’s tree-lighting. articles.text: Editor: When Proposition 13 passed in 1978, California’s K-12 public schools lost $3 billion in funding overnight. In recent years, the California Budget and Policy Center found that California ranked: • 41st in K-12 spending per student • Last in the number of K-12 students per teacher • Last in the number of K-12 students per guidance counselor • Last in the number of K-12 students per librarian Proposition 15 on November’s ballot would have raised an estimated $6.5 to $11.5 billion annually in revenues for the State’s K-12 schools and community colleges, counties, cities, and special districts. Proposition 15 failed to pass. For the 2021-2022 school year, despite state and local funding including revenue from Measures G&H, the Piedmont Unified School District (PUSD) will have a shortfall of $1,930 per student. If the Piedmont Education Foundation did not exist, this would be the unfortunate financial reality for our schools and our students. For the last 45 years PEF has raised money from our generous community to help bridge the gap between state and local funding and what it costs to provide an excellent education to our students. The result is that PUSD has been able to lower class sizes, ensure crucial classroom aides and student support, offer AP courses, art, music, science and other vital curriculum to students, and have the resources to keep Piedmont schools as among the highest rated in the State. Regardless of the administration of PUSD, changes in approaches to K-12 education, fluctuations in student enrollment, economic recessions -- and even a global pandemic -- PEF remains steadfast in its mission. It is nonpartisan and focused. Its only mission is to fundraise and foster community engagement in support of Piedmont schools. Please separate any perspectives on how PUSD is navigating in-person or distance learning from the purpose of PEF’s Giving Campaign. The financial outlook for K-12 public schools in California has not changed under the COVID-19 pandemic. Some argue that without intervention, it will become worse. Withholding a Giving Campaign contribution today only sets the district back in its capacity to provide the highest level of education to our students during the next school year. Instead, let’s step up to support our schools and give them the resources they need to be ready for our students next fall, arguably after one of the most challenging academic years they will experience. articles.text: November 23 was worst day in county history for pandemic On Monday, November 23, a total of 547 new cases of COVID- 19 were reported in Alameda County, the highest number of cases added in a single day in the county. The pandemic is surging in recent weeks on a scale not seen since August, according to Alameda County Public Health Department data. The current spike is poised to be worse than this past summer. On Saturday, November 28, an additional 312 new cases were recorded in the county. Previously, the worst day for the county was 417 cases on August 13. The county’s case rate is now 9.1 cases per 100,000 people. The rising case rate caused the state to put the entire county, which includes Piedmont, into the Purple Tier this month. The Purple Tier, or Widespread Tier, is the most restrictive tier of the state’s color-coded four-tiered system. According to the state, counties are placed in the Purple Tier when the case rate is over 7 per 100,000 people. Overall in Alameda County, the rolling seven-day positive percentage for COVID-19 tests is currently 3.7 percent, a metric that has swelled upward across the past week. The total caseload in Alameda County is now 29,865, an increase of over 2,000 cases from one week ago, the ACPHD reported yesterday, Tuesday, December 1. Tragically, 15 more people have died of COVID-19 in the county, bringing the total number of fatalities to 514. No new cases of COVID-19 were reported amongst Piedmonters over the past seven days. There have been 65 cases of COVID-19 in Piedmont since the pandemic began. In Oakland, the most populous city in Alameda County, the number of cases has now reached 10,777. In Hayward, 4,519 cases have been recorded and there have been 2,247 reported in Fremont. San Leandro reported 1,712, Livermore reported 1,365, Union City reported 1,215 and Berkeley reported 1,158. The county enacted Purple Tier restrictions for business and activities on Wednesday, November 18. Health officials across the Bay Area have hinted that new lockdown orders could be on the horizon as cases continue to rise. articles.text: Wildwood Ave., Requa Rd., Hill Lane on city’s list The City of Piedmont expects to receive bids in January to repave several stretches of roadway next summer. On November 2, the City Council agreed to pay $122,570 for engineering proposals for the projects. The Public Works Department expects the work to primarily include roadway resurfacing and the replacement of certain curbs, gutters and sidewalks. Some 15 new pedestrian ramps will be added to City sidewalks. Two portions of Wildwood Avenue are slated to be repaved – a portion from Grand Avenue to Nova Road and then a longer span from Prospect Avenue to Highland Avenue. “Crossing modifications” to improve pedestrian safety will be added at the T-intersection of Wildwood and Highland Avenues, according to a report from Chester Nakahara, Director of Public Works. Nearly all of Requa Road, from Hazel Avenue to Wildwood Avenue, will be repaved. A portion of Grand Avenue between Wildwood Avenue to Fairview Drive will be repaved. Concrete bulb-outs, new pedestrian crossing signs and flashing beacons will be added to the crosswalk in front of Ace Hardware. All of these improvements were proposed as part of the City’s Pedestrian/Bicycle Master Plan. The span of Hampton Road between Glen Alpine Road and St. James Avenue will also be repaved, and new bike lanes will be installed. The City is still deciding on the nature of these bike lanes, which may necessitate the elimination of some on-street parking on Hampton Road. The City will be seeking input from residents, the Pedestrian & Bicycle Advisory Committee and Council on the issue. A full repaving of Hill Lane is being planned. It is an alley between Nova and Arbor Drive. Workers will have to bore through the roadway of Hill Lane for samples to determine the health of the underlying substrate. “This will help to determine the appropriate rehabilitation method that will be necessary,” Nakahara wrote in his report to council. Council last month approved a payment of $122,570 to Coastland Engineers for engineering services to plan the 2021 repaving projects. Coastland outlined a proposal in October. Money for Coastland Engineering’s work will come from Measure B funds. Nakahara said that construction drawings, specifications and bid documents will be completed in January of 2021. The project will go out to bid soon after Council approval of these documents. The City plans to start the repaving work in the middle of June, 2021. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. City plans for 2021 summer street paving Wildwood Ave., Requa Rd., Hill Lane on city’s list By Barry Eitel The City of Piedmont expects to receive bids in January to repave several stretches of roadway next summer. On November 2, the City Council agreed to pay $122,570 for engineering proposals for the projects. The Public Works Department expects the work to primarily include roadway resurfacing and the replacement of certain curbs, gutters and sidewalks. Some 15 new pedestrian ramps will be added to City sidewalks. Two portions of Wildwood Avenue are slated to be repaved – a portion from Grand Avenue to Nova Road and then a longer span from Prospect Avenue to Highland Avenue. “Crossing modifications” to improve pedestrian safety will be added at the T-intersection of Wildwood and Highland Avenues, according to a report from Chester Nakahara, Director of Public Works. Nearly all of Requa Road, from Hazel Avenue to Wildwood Avenue, will be repaved. A portion of Grand Avenue between Wildwood Avenue to Fairview Drive will be repaved. Concrete bulb-outs, new pedestrian crossing signs and flashing beacons will be added to the crosswalk in front of Ace Hardware. All of these improvements were proposed as part of the City’s Pedestrian/Bicycle Master Plan. The span of Hampton Road between Glen Alpine Road and St. James Avenue will also be repaved, and new bike lanes will be installed. The City is still deciding on the nature of these bike lanes, which may necessitate the elimination of some on-street parking on Hampton Road. The City will be seeking input from residents, the Pedestrian & Bicycle Advisory Committee and Council on the issue. A full repaving of Hill Lane is being planned. It is an alley between Nova and Arbor Drive. Workers will have to bore through the roadway of Hill Lane for samples to determine the health of the underlying substrate. “This will help to determine the appropriate rehabilitation method that will be necessary,” Nakahara wrote in his report to council. Council last month approved a payment of $122,570 to Coastland Engineers for engineering services to plan the 2021 repaving projects. Coastland outlined a proposal in October. Money for Coastland Engineering’s work will come from Measure B funds. Nakahara said that construction drawings, specifications and bid documents will be completed in January of 2021. The project will go out to bid soon after Council approval of these documents. The City plans to start the repaving work in the middle of June, 2021. articles.text: For 36 years the Piedmont Scouts BSA has collected food and funds to help feed families in Alameda County. All food and funds are given to the Alameda County Food Bank. Piedmont residents were especially generous last year, donating 8,095 pounds of food and $6,215 in cash to the Food Bank. This year they have already exceeded the goal of raising $7,500. Instead of a one-day annual food collection drive, this year’s campaign has been extended for five weeks, from November 1 through December 6. In addition, every Tuesday is Giving Back Tuesday. “We hope that those who have so generously donated food in the past will give online this year to help us combat food insecurity,” said Katy Kobal, Piedmont’s Scouting for Food Chair. Every dollar donated allows the Food Bank to purchase $7 worth of food. “We estimate that our need has doubled in Alameda county,” said Suzan Bateson, Executive Director of the Alameda County Community Food Bank. “October was our biggest month in food distribution ever. We anticipated distributing five million pounds of food. That is record-breaking.” Pre-COVID, Alameda County had one of the highest incidences of hunger in the nation. Nearly 20 percent of residents in the county live below the poverty line. Of those receiving assistance from the Alameda County Food Bank, two-thirds are children and the elderly. Donate online today by going to https://tinyurl.com/scoutingforfood2020 and turn $1 into $7 of food. For details, contact Morgan Fjord at the Scout office at 510-844-4752.

articles.text: Superintendent Randy Booker sent out an email Monday evening announcing a town hall meeting will be held prior to Winter Break to address secondary school parents’ questions and give more information about school reopening. The meeting will be held through Zoom with Superintendent Booker, and secondary school principals. The school district has not confirmed the date and time, but it will likely take place the week of December 14. Demand for a public forum resulted largely from a survey sent out by Booker to parents of students in grades 6-12 asking for in-person or distance learning preference. With little previous public discussion, the survey asked parents that chose Distance Learning to sign off on a move to bring in an independent company, Edgenuity. What troubled many parents was that the Edgenuity Virtual Academy was only mentioned after starting the survey. Parents that only read the email and didn’t get deep into the survey would not know any detail about the Edgenuity online program. At least one school board member acknowledged that it was an error to spring the implementation of Edgenuity onto parents in the survey. The district will not use Edgenuity for 100 percent distance learning. If families and counselors want, on a case-bycase basis individual students can use the platform. Due to parents’ feedback, Booker closed the survey and now has called for a town hall-style public meeting prior to reissuing a new survey. In the initial survey it was revealed that distance learners would “receive the bulk of instruction in a variety of courses using an Edgenuity product “Courseware.’” For parents, one of the troubling portions of the survey included this description: “With a variety of course needs, the facilitation teacher may not be an expert in the course materials, so as an additional support, course specific live tutors are available on the platform.” “I was disheartened to see a move that put the quality of secondary student education in harm’s way without public debate by the school board,” said parent Hari Titan. “A major change to an online virtual academy typically is months in the making with an advisory board and multiple school board meetings. That did not happen this time. Instead, this major paradigm shift was buried deep in a survey given to secondary school parents.” The Edgenuity program is not planned to be discussed by administrators or board members in the Town Hall meeting. An e-mail on December 1 by Booker stated, “Distance learning students will receive instruction by a certified teacher.” The public meeting will address progress on “teachers and staff identifying various learning models, including piloting cameras to support a ‘concurrent classroom’ model for our program,” according to Booker. In-person classes could utilize filmed sessions live-streamed to students either in the other cohort, in quarantine or choosing distance learning. Other school districts have implemented or plan to use class filming, however, privacy issues must be addressed. As Alameda County currently is in the purple tier of COVID restrictions, in-person learning cannot begin until clearance is given by the Alameda County Public Health Department. Current restrictions require counties to move in the red tier before reopening schools. As of December 1, 52 of 58 of California’s counties are in the purple tier, including 99.2 percent of the state’s population. articles.text: On November 20 the Oakland Zoo opened its gates to nighttime visitors for the brand new event “GLOWFARI-a wildly illuminating lantern festival.” GLOWFARI takes the place of Zoolights which has been a zoo tradition for two decades. GLOWFARI features larger light display lanterns, longer hours, and more available dates than Zoolights. Hundreds of larger than life animal lanterns illuminate the milelong stroll that is truly an event fun for all ages. The brilliantly-lit gondola will be open to provide access to the California Trail and its vast views of the bay. The trail atop the gondola has turned into the Land of the Lost, filled with huge dinosaur lanterns and life-like animatronic moving models of dinos like the T-rex, stegosaurus, and triceratops. “It was very important to offer something to people to get away and have an emotional break from the stress of this year’s daily challenges,” said the Zoo’s VP of Marketing and Communications Erin Harrison. Signs all through the park educate guests on animals’ status in the wild, what people can do to help, and the challenges each species face. Capacity is limited to around 1,500 and guests have been vigilantly abiding to the mask and social distancing requirements. articles.text: A time of year to remember to shop locally Piedmont Avenue businesses that have struggled to stay in business will soon see relief with all stores being open during the holiday season. Due to the COVID epidemic, there won’t be a Holiday Stroll, or the traditional tree lighting ceremony at Key Route Plaza on Piedmont Avenue & 41st Street. “We are not doing the tree lighting this year,” confirmed retailer Philippa Roberts. “It takes a lot of time and money, neither of which is very abundant these days.” Businesses desperately need a strong holiday season this year. Most have had to be creative to save their businesses. Claudio Luporini, owner of Bella Ceramica and a personal friend of Kris Kringle, said that Santa will have to skip his annual trip to the Avenue due to the coronavirus health restrictions in place. However, Luporini as always, will provide egg nog, hot totties, hot cocoa, bubbly, and cookies for customers. Nathan Walden, owner of Nathan & Co. with locations on Piedmont Ave. and College Ave., has been busy adapting to the times. For Black Friday – the Friday after Thanksgiving – and the following week, if customers say they are friends of Oakland Tech High School or Claremont Middle School, 20 percent of the sale will go to the Teacher’s Association for that school. Nathan and Co. was quick to jump on a new platform called www.KeepOaklandAlive.com. The website has teamed up with the most popular stores in Oakland by offering free two-day delivery. The fabric of the community lies at stake this holiday season, local business have ramped up their online and curbside pickup options to do what they can to keep people engaged and safe. “Rest assured, Piedmont Avenue is open and ready for business,” said longtime Piedmont Ave. volunteer Ronile Lahti. “Our holiday shopping message is Shop Local, Shop Oakland, but Shop Piedmont Avenue first. If we don’t have it, we’ll do our best to find it for you.” – Ronile Lahti Piedmont Ave. volunteer “The whole year has been just a huge challenge. We are concentrating on PR and pushing our website. I have brought back a publicist to help drive traffic to the website to bring in some dollars, but business is still down 50 percent.” Walden has kept his commitments to the community however.

articles.text: The California Interscholastic Federation made two major announcements yesterday, Tuesday, December 1. In addition to postponing its official scheduled start of practice for winter sports on December 7, the CIF canceled regional and state playoffs for the year. Th sports affected are football, cross country, water polo, and boys volleyball. “The CIF State Office is removing all Regional and State Championship events from the Season 1 Sports calendar. By canceling Regional and State Championship events, more student-athletes will have the opportunity to participate in a longer season, rather than a truncated season with Regional and State post-season play for a limited number of schools,” wrote the federation in its press release. The CIF said it would not “issue any guidance” until after January 1 – at least – in response to the California Department of Public Health not issuing any updates on youth sports in its recent announcement. “Due to the continued surge in COVID-19 infections, the California Department of Public Health has postponed the issuance of its updated youth sports guidance. The CIF does not expect the CDPH will issue any guidance allowing for schools to return to full practice and competition until after January 1, 2021, at the earliest. Thus, all full practice and competition start dates are officially on hold until updated guidance is issued,” wrote the CIF. The head of the California Department of Public Health is the former Aameda County Public Health Director. Additionally, the CIF moved boys’ volleyball – which would have new at Piedmont High in the spring – to its Season 2 alongside the other chunk of sports like basketball, soccer, lacrosse, baseball, softball, track, swimming, golf, and badminton. The cancelation of the postseason means there will be no North Coast Section playoffs for football, cross country, or water polo, The Cross Country State Championship, the state’s oldest sports championship, has been called off. Photos courtesy of CIF The California Interscholastic Federation announced on Tuesday, December 1 that it is postponing the official start of high school practices and canceling its playoffs tournaments. North Coast Section playoffs have been abandoned for football, water polo, cross country, and girls’ volleyball. Cross-country may be the sport most affected by the change, as runners typically put in their fastest times at the NCS Meet of Champions in an effort to qualify for state. Without a regional postseason, this means that the Western Alameda County Conference could theoretically schedule more games for its 12-team conference. Piedmont football team was initially set to open its non-conference schedule on January 8 in a traditional game with Justin-Siena of Napa, with successive games each week until February’s league schedule in the WACC. “The CIF is confident this decision is a necessary and reasonable action for our member schools, student-athletes, and school communities in light of the current statewide crisis. This revision to the CIF State 2020-21 Season 1 Sports calendar offers our Sections and Leagues the flexibility and needed time to plan for the return to practice and competition once updated guidance is provided by the CDPH,” wrote the CIF.

articles.text: Western Alameda County Conference (WACC) commissioner Dave Kiesel voiced uncertainty around the California Interscholastic Federation’s sports schedule last week, saying his office has not yet received clarification from the CIF. “All they’ve said is that they’ll let you know when we know,” Kiesel said in an interview with the Mercury News. “I guess that’s the part that’s frustrating our athletic directors and our principals and our coaches in our schools – they don’t know when they’re going to know… So who knows what’s going to happen? It’s all a big question mark. All we know now is what we can’t do.” Staff Photos – League Commissioner Dave Kiesel Asked about whether schools are frustrated by the lack of clarification from the CIF, Kiesel said that WACC is “not ready” for the federation’s scheduled start of practice on December 7, given their lack of planning thus far. “There’s been frustration. Sixteen-year-olds don’t want to be told what they can’t do… The problem for them, and for coaches and athletic directors that represent them, is that there is frustration because everyone’s saying, ‘Well, you can’t do this, you can’t do that.’ That’s from school boards and school districts, or counties or the NCS, the CIF, or the State Department of Health,” he said. “They’re certainly aware of the seriousness of the virus, and they’re certainly not interested in doing stuff they shouldn’t be doing. But it’s just really difficult to plan if you don’t know how you’re going to plan, if you don’t Newly designated winter sports, including football, are scheduled to start practice on December 7. have a calendar for planning. I don’t think anyone believes we’re going to start practice on Dec. 7. I think that’s just not going to happen. We’re not ready for it, and no one wants to do it if it can’t be done in a safe manner, and (it’s) pretty evident now that it can’t be done in a safe manner.” Kiesel reiterated that he has “no idea” when he will receive an official plan or schedule information from CIF officials, who have repeatedly said they’ll advise the league when able to. “No idea. Again, all they’ve said is that they’ll let you know when we know. I guess that’s the part that’s frustrating our athletic directors and our principals and our coaches in our schools, is that they don’t know when they’re going to know,” said Kiesel. Piedmont High’s sports programs returned for its conditioning programs ahead of the 2021 schedule only a couple of days prior to Alameda County going back to the Purple Tier if CIVUD restrictions. Kiesel said each school district will dictate whether teams can continue practicing. “We’re all in Alameda County, and Alameda County has gone back to (the restrictive purple tier). That’s up to the individual districts to make that decision. But the kids are ready to participate in physical activity, whether they’re ready to participate in a game or not is really questionable because they haven’t done much for three months from a physical point of view. Everyone’s being cautious.” Although Kiesel added that he’s been impressed with the schools which are conditioning, like Piedmont, he is unsure of “how long that’s going to last” with the new restrictive measures. “I believe we have seven schools that are doing this now. I was really impressed by the safety precautions the various schools have put into effect in terms of the treatment of pods, the size of pods and the involvement of lots of school personnel to make sure the kids are doing what they’re supposed to be doing. I don’t know how long that’s going last,” he said. Kiesel added that he is unsure whether school football programs will be able to accomplish a 10-game season as planned. The WACC, which has 12 schools, still plans on merging with the eight-team Mission Valley Athletic League for the football season to form three divisions: Foothill, Shoreline, and Mission. Kiesel mentioned that the MVAL and WACC could work together on other sports because they are are close together geographically. Schools in the MVAL include Sourthern Alameda County high schools: American, Irvington, Kennedy, Mission, and Washington, Moreau, Newark Memorial and James Logan. Dave Kiesel mentioned that PHS is among seven schools that returned to non-sports specific training.

articles.text: Maradona passes away at age 60; Diop at 42 The International soccer world is mourning the loss of two of its most brilliant stars who passed away this week. Argentinian legend Diego Maradona passed away on November 25 due to a heart attack at age 60, while Senegalese star Papa Bouba Diop succumbed to ALS on November 29. He was only 42. Maradona’s illustrious career started at Argentinos Juniors and Boca Juniors from 1976-1982 before transferring to Barcelona on a world record free of $7.6 million until he requested a move in 1984 after a violent brawl with Athletic Bilbao, It resulted in his polarizing trade to Napoli for a record $10.48 million. Naples at the time was considered among the poorest cities in Italy, leading to assumptions that local mafia groups helped finance the purchase of Maradona’s contract. In the 1980s Maradonna’s arrival in Naples had a polarizing impact on the wealthier northern cities and the poorer residents of Italy’s southern peninsula. But from then on, Maradona became Naples’ favorite son. Local journalists called him a savior. They noted that the city lacked a “mayor, houses, schools, buses, employment and sanitation. None of this matters because we have Maradona.” He led Napoli to its only Serie A titles, in 1987 and 1990, while their UEFA Cup title in 1989 is its only major European championship. It took the organization 24 years to win another Coppa Italia after Maradona’s in ’87 and likewise for its Suppercoppa Italiana in 1990, not earning it again until 2014. For Argentina’s National Team, Maradona is popularly known for the “Hand of God” goal in their 2-1 win over England in the 1986 World Cup quarterfinals, where he controversially used his hand to score the winning goal – but referees, out of position without a clear view, allowed the score. Following the game, Maradona said the goal was “a little with the head, and a little with the hand of God.” It was voted the Goal of the Century by FIFA in 2002. Argentina went on to win the 1986 World Cup Finals 3-2 over West Germany. They lost in the 1990 Finals 1-0 in a rematch with West Germany. But one cannot mention Maradona and his death without also acknowledging his battles along the way. He suffered from drug addiction during his playing days Photo courtesy of CBS Sports Diego Maradona is shown in 1986 after Argentina won the World Cup. It is the last time Argentina won the acclaimed trophy. with Napoli and after his retirement. He was also diagnosed with hepatitis as a result of alcohol dependence later in life. He underwent emergency brain surgery on November 2 to treat subdural hematoma and was released 10 days later. Weeks later on November 25, Maradona suffered a fatal heart attack at his home in Argentina. Papa Bouba Diop, 42 Diop was an influential star for generations of African footballers. He is best known for his contributions to the Senegalese National Team where he made 63 total appearances at center back and central defense midfield. Diop, towering at 6 feet, 5 inches, was nicknamed “The Wardrobe” due to his ability to cover the midfield. The highlight of his career came in Senegal’s World Cup debut in 2002. He scored the game-winning goal in a 1-0 upset victory over defending champion France in the Group Stage, which ultimately eliminated Les Bleus from the tournament. In the Round of 16, Senegal upset Sweden with a 20-year old Zlatan Ibrahimovic in a classic 2-1 win in extra time. Senegal, The Lions of Teranga, danced on the field in celebration. Diop was also a mainstay throughout major European leagues. He made 47 appearances with France’s Ligue 1’s Lens from 2002-2004 before making his way to Fulham in England’s Premier League until 2007. After a stint in EPL club Portsmouth from 2007-2010, he eventually finished his career in AEK Athens of Greece for two seasons, returned to England’s West Ham United for 2011 and 2012, and Birmingham City until 2013. Diop died in Paris on November 29 of complications from the disease ALS (Lou Gehrig’s Disease). Photo courtesy of Sky Sports Papa Bouba Diop with the Senegal National Team.

articles.text: California’s woes came back to haunt them in a disastrous Big Game for the Golden Bears, allowing a blocked extra point attempt with the game at 24-23 with 58 seconds left. Cal was seemingly set to force overtime against the Stanford Cardinal, but Stanford won its 10th victory in 11 Big Games. Adding insult to injury, Cal’s sound system inadvertently played its fight song in anticipation of a converted field goal as Stanford celebrated its block. Like California playing their song after a tragedy, nothing has gone as expected this season. Cal sits at 0-3 with a roster full of upperclassmen and a string of COVID-19 infections; Stanford is now 1-2 after its program also had its run-in with the virus. Down 24-17 with 3:30 left in the game, the Golden Bears marched 90 yards to cap off a drive with Chris Brown Jr. to make it 24-23. But Cal’s special teams unit has shown in thre games that it struggles to handle the most basic of requirements. Cal, notably had a COVID run in with its offensive line and have had depleted numbers. In addition to the blocked PAT, it had a blocked 32-yard field goal attempt, and fumbled a punt return by Nikko Remigio. It also allowed a blocked punt in their 31-27 loss to Oregon State. Cal is set to face No. 23 Oregon this Saturday, and easily to go to an 0-4 record. The Cardinal wins the Axe in Big Game Stanford QB Davis Mills got the job done with 24 completions for 205 yards and a touchdown. Cardinal sophomore and former Bishop O’Dowd running back Austin Jones had a big day with 85 yards and two touchdowns on 21 attempts. It was his career-high. But it was defensive lineman Thomas Booker who increased his draft stock as a disruptive rusher with two blocked field goals against Cal. Stanford is set to face No. 22 Washington on Saturday and will be the underdogs. But because Stanford is in Santa Clara County, its team will not be able to practice in Palo Alto due to new COVID health restrictions. The team is considering staying in the Pacific Northwest after its game with the Huskies and preparing there for its season-finale against Oregon State on December 12. Photo courtesy of Sports radio service Stanford’s Austin Jones (20), a Bishop O’Dowd alum, ran for 85 yards and scored two touchdowns. Photo courtesy of AP Cal long snapper Slater Zellers sits in frustration after the field goal team allowed its PAT kick to be blocked.

articles.text: Playwright Loy A. Webb’s The Light will be presented by Shotgun Players December 4-13. Berkeley-based Shotgun Players is presenting The Light live streamed December 4-13 on Youtube. articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse is presenting Brian Copeland’s The Jewelry Box, available to stream through December 25. The comedy is a prequel to Copeland’s hit solo show, Not a Genuine Black Man, and follows young protagonist Brian as he heads to the “mean streets” of Oakland to buy his mom a Christmas present. articles.text: The new reality in classical music is virtual, with a totally new genre of concert: close-knit ensembles playing, even though they might never meet each other. The San Francisco Symphony tackled the mid-pandemic problem with an elaborate, costly, hi-tech solution to bring forth an hour-long prerecorded program crackling with energy, talent, modernity and diversity, filmed in part “around the world,” per drum-beating press release. Featured with the classical players were contrasting figures rarely in the concert hall, like rap artists and a barefoot jazz singer also playing contrabass – double duty. And an array entirely of living composers, including one world premiere. All available for you indefinitely by streaming. What more could one ask for? In effect, this concert forced musicians onto another planet, well out of their comfort zone. If it was challenging, it was just the beginning during this seemingly endless pandemic: Either sepa- – and to the smattering of SFS players featured. With discreet social distancing and masking de rigeur for one and all. Close performer teamwork, despite wide separation. The sophisticated video-shoot technique readily combined a half-dozen instrumentalists in a single mosaic-like image, coming from equally remote locations in close coordination, with all wearing earphones to catch the unifying beat – solos, duets, sometimes close to a dozen together. articles.text: A scene from Avegners: Endgame featuring an all-star cast. Movie review by Chris Honoré Avengers: Endgame. So, this is how it ends… a rockin’ franchise of 22 connected installments, replete with superheroes and astonishingly crowded with imagination and let’er rip, stand alone narratives wherein the only way Marvel Studios can construct a spectrum brand is to call it the Marvel Comic Universe (MCU). Okay, grandiose perhaps, but somehow nicely comprehensive. Think of MCU as a panoply of cosmic players – beginning with Iron Man (Robert Downey), Captain America (Chris Evans), the Incredible Hulk (Mark Ruffalo), Thor (Chris Hemsworth), Ant-Man (Paul Rudd) – all outrageously brimming with skill sets, bionic bespoke gear/suits / weaponry, each displaying swagger with attitude, and, in the case of Endgame, buttressed by space (and time) travel that not only thrills but resonates. In the aggregate It’s extraordinary. Pedestrian and mysterious, perhaps, to some cinephiles, but nevertheless there it is. Blockbusters R-US. And fundamentally, it’s the word “resonates” that interests and compels. It’s not just a universe of art and stories displayed in panels of vibrant colors, text, and bubble dialogue, displayed with a delineated genius. These are mythic stories that have a certain power and are taken to the silver screen where each tale is adapted and then enhanced by CGI, which means that now, today, and going forward, if the writers, directors, and cinematographers can imagine it, the filmmakers can seamlessly create it. And that has made all the difference. The embedded question that Endgame asks, as does every superhero comic ever produced by Marvel or DC, dating back to the 1930s, is: How do we understand what there is about superhero archetypes that so compel. What causes this response, this need to construct a universe overlay of fandom, one that ensnares so completely that nearly a century of illustrated magazines (and now films) has morphed into this massive body of work, which defies the gravity of pop culture fickleness and instead has managed to follow an arc that continues to trend upward. It’s remarkable. To restate the plot of Endgame, heavy with predicates, it does connect directly to Infinity Wars, picking up where the latter left off. For those steeped in MCU culture are definitely up to speed and need no tutorial regarding who is who and where is where, including the why of it all – from the profoundly genocidal Thanos, to Captain America, to Thor, Hulk, Black Widow, Hawkeye, Rocket, and, of course, Ant-Man. Suffice it to say that they team up for an epic do-over/time travel journey, their mission to alter decisively what is referred to by some as Thanos’ “Snapture” wherein he vanishes half of all the inhabitants of the universe using “six infinity stones.” Any story involving time travel is tricky, a sort of Mobius strip script, so to speak. Problems will arise that often elude simple solutions – characters meet themselves and so on – but not only are such moments adequately resolved in Endgame, they offer some comedy relief (in one long scene, Captain America faces off against Captain America), as well as a running montage of best scenes from stories past. Avengers: Endgame is three hours long, amounting to a galactic Ben Hur without an intermission. But the story engages from the get-go and doesn’t let up. Of course, exposition has never been the dominant mode chosen to move any MCU plot along. The final question to be asked is this: is this symphony of a finale the end of the beginning, or the beginning of the end? Best bet: it’s not over until it’s over and the spirit of Stan Lee, et al. lives in the MCU. Avengers: Endgame. Directed by Anthony Russo and Joe Russo. Starring Robert Downey, Chris Evans and Scarlett Johansson. 120 min. Rated PG-13. A scene from Avegners: Endgame.
articles.title: MOVIES FOR ADULTS Avengers: Endgame a brilliant finale – or is it?

articles.text: Carey Mulligan stars in Suffragette. Movie review by Chris Honoré Though the film Suffragette takes place over 100 years ago (1912-1913), and though its core issue, that of a woman’s right to vote, has long ago been settled, the narrative in this 2015 British historical drama still feels contemporary and relevant. A century has indeed passed, yet we know that women today still struggle for equal pay and job opportunities and, of course, the ultimate control of their bodies. What has been dimmed by the passage of time are the harrowing risks women took as they did battle with an iron-fisted, often misogynistic patriarchy that was committed to preventing them from acquiring the right to vote. It is through the eyes of Maud Watts (Carey Mulligan), an English working class woman, who works 12-hour days in a large factory-like laundry, washing and ironing other people’s clothes, that the story is told. In act one, Maud, who leads an insulated, narrow life – she’s married and has a son – is terrified when she finds herself on a London street and is unexpectedly swept up in a demonstration by suffragettes who are insisting on the right to vote. Suddenly Maud finds herself surrounded by women who are prepared to confront the police, feel the pain of their clubs, and endure arrest and weeks of incarceration for a cause in which they passionately believe. These courageous women are a revelation to Maud. She has long felt oppressed and treated as if she were mere property to be used and then disposed of by men. Abruptly the scales fall from her eyes and her consciousness is raised. A scene from Avegners: Endgame featuring an all-star cast. Movie review by Chris Honoré Avengers: Endgame. So, this is how it ends… a rockin’ franchise of 22 connected installments, replete with superheroes and astonishingly crowded with imagination and let’er rip, stand alone narratives wherein the only way Marvel Studios can construct a spectrum brand is to call it the Marvel Comic Universe (MCU). Okay, grandiose perhaps, but somehow nicely comprehensive. Think of MCU as a panoply of cosmic players – beginning with Iron Man (Robert Downey), Captain America (Chris Evans), the Incredible Hulk (Mark Ruffalo), Thor (Chris Hemsworth), Ant-Man (Paul Rudd) – all outrageously brimming with skill sets, bionic bespoke gear/suits / weaponry, each displaying swagger with attitude, and, in the case of Endgame, buttressed by space (and time) travel that not only thrills but resonates. In the aggregate It’s extraordinary. Pedestrian and mysterious, perhaps, to some cinephiles, but nevertheless there it is. Blockbusters R-US. And fundamentally, it’s the word “resonates” that interests and compels. It’s not just a universe of art and stories displayed in panels of vibrant colors, text, and bubble dialogue, displayed with a delineated genius. These are mythic stories that have a certain power and are taken to the silver screen where each tale is adapted and then enhanced by CGI, which means that now, today, and going forward, if the writers, directors, and cinematographers can imagine it, the filmmakers can seamlessly create it. And that has made all the difference. The embedded question that Endgame asks, as does every superhero comic ever produced by Marvel or DC, dating back to the 1930s, is: How do we understand what there is about superhero archetypes that so compel. What causes this response, this need to construct a universe overlay of fandom, one that ensnares so completely that nearly a century of illustrated magazines (and now films) has morphed into this massive body of work, which defies the gravity of pop culture fickleness and instead has managed to follow an arc that continues to trend upward. It’s remarkable. To restate the plot of Endgame, heavy with predicates, it does connect directly to Infinity Wars, picking up where the latter left off. For those steeped in MCU culture are definitely up to speed and need no tutorial regarding who is who and where is where, including the why of it all – from the profoundly genocidal Thanos, to Captain America, to Thor, Hulk, Black Widow, Hawkeye, Rocket, and, of course, Ant-Man. Suffice it to say that they team up for an epic do-over/time travel journey, their mission to alter decisively what is referred to by some as Thanos’ “Snapture” wherein he vanishes half of all the inhabitants of the universe using “six infinity stones.” Any story involving time travel is tricky, a sort of Mobius strip script, so to speak. Problems will arise that often elude simple solutions – characters meet themselves and so on – but not only are such moments adequately resolved in Endgame, they offer some comedy relief (in one long scene, Captain America faces off against Captain America), as well as a running montage of best scenes from stories past. Avengers: Endgame is three hours long, amounting to a galactic Ben Hur without an intermission. But the story engages from the get-go and doesn’t let up. Of course, exposition has never been the dominant mode chosen to move any MCU plot along. The final question to be asked is this: is this symphony of a finale the end of the beginning, or the beginning of the end? Best bet: it’s not over until it’s over and the spirit of Stan Lee, et al. lives in the MCU. Avengers: Endgame. Directed by Anthony Russo and Joe Russo. Porco (Michael Keaton) was an ace Italian flyer during World War I, and was known then as Marco Pagot. Porco is a mercenary- bounty hunter pilot, hired to fight the menacing air pirates (aka Mamma Aiuto) who roam the local skies. In Milan he meets a young girl, Flo (Kimberly Willia Paisley), who happens to be an airplane mechanic and engineer. Porco hires her to fix his plane. articles.text: Somewhere awhile back I read: If there is one building alone in a field, there is Architecture; if there are two buildings, we have urban design. I’ve always thought this a good summary definition or description of an essential discipline that makes up our built environment. In the design world it can often be simply stated as the arrangement of various buildings and the design of the spaces between them. It inevitably applies to all scales of development, from the highly urban downtown San Francisco’s new Transbay Terminal and garden neighborhood, to small residential cities like Piedmont. (A visit to this remarkable work of urban design at the Transbay Terminal and garden early on a Sunday is well worth it. Drive and park right outside on the street. It is not crowded, is staffed by the city, and is accessible and free.) Good Urban Design is the secret to what makes vital, real “places” instead of just a collection of buildings. It is my opinion that this important design consideration is not well understood and has been, at best, a disappointment throughout our country for many decades. Focus has been on individual buildings, but the public spaces that link them – the urban design – has too often been poorly designed or even completely neglected. In Piedmont there seems to be a strong awareness of this important concept. Although our urban design considerations are not as dramatic as large, dense urban areas, they are, like everywhere, essential in the creation of places that foster community. Our General Plan, Zoning Code, and Design Review Process are the tools with which we deal with the preservation and enhancement of the relationships between buildPiedmont’s iconic Exedra Plaza is an excellent example of meaningful Urban Design. Combining the disciplines of planning, architecture, and landscape architecture, it is wonderfully proportioned, placed to terminate the visual axis of Highland Ave and located to provide a landmark, a meeting place, a venue for various events and is as a result, a place that fosters community.

articles.text: It’s hard to imagine how much wine is made in the Languedoc region of France. Curving along the Mediterranean from Provence to close to the Spanish border it is a vast, wild area covered with grape vines that were first planted by the Romans two thousand years ago. It is often combined with Roussillon, its neighbor to the south. Together they have 700,000 acres of vines, the biggest vineyard area in the world - producing more wine than the entire U.S. For many years, the wines were churned out by co-operatives and the emphasis was more on quantity than quality. Any grocery store in France will feature hundreds of bottles of Languedoc wine starting at 2 euros. But the exciting story in Languedoc is the emergence over the past two decades of many artisan winemakers who care deeply about the quality of their wines and whose finest examples can compete with any wine region in France. It’s good news for the consumer because the reputation has not quite caught up with the wines; they still represent remarkable bargains selling in the U.S. for between $10 and $20. This month we will explore my very favorite Languedoc producer. (The best way to find these wines is to use the Wine Searcher app.) Domaine La Tour Boisee I have twice had the opportunity to visit this charming winery located in the small village of Laure Minervois. The property includes part of a medieval stone wall and tower that gives the winery its name. We were greeted by Jean-Louis Poudou. the owner, and Florence Hallett, the gracious business manager who walked us through the lineup of about 13 wines. Winery Owner Jean-Louis Poudou. The 2017 Marie-Claude Chateau Tour Boisee Minervois. The flagship wine is the 2017 Minervois Cuvee Marie-Claude an inky monster that has a rich blueberry nose that leaps from the glass. In the mouth it is rich and full bursting with blackberry fruit and finishing with firm tannins. I brought this wine to a blind tasting recently and it killed wines four times more costly. Available for less than 15 Euros. it is a remarkable value. Another killer wine from Tour Boisee is the 2018 Carignan from 60-year-old vines. It is rich, complex, dark and opulent. It oozes dark berry fruit and has a smooth, soft finish. This has become my house wine. Everyone I have poured it for has ended up buying a case. Amazingly it is available on the internet for around $10 a bottle. A value like this does my French/Scottish heart good. The winery has come out with a new label since I first visited. The 2019 Un Historie de Famille is a blend of Grenache, Domaine La Tour Boisee in the village of Laure Minervois, France.

articles.text: Photo by Deborah Quok This Pear-Cranberry Upside-Down Cake is an ideal treat for the holidays. The 2020 Holiday Season will be different for most of us – scaled back. Or way back in the case of our family. I usually bake volumes whilst we enjoy gatherings with friends and family. Sometimes my holiday baking projects are fancy but most of the time they are a simple presentation. This pear-cranberry upsidedown cake manages to be both stunning and simple. It is perfect for any time of day. Pear-Cranberry Upside-Down Cake Inspired by Alice Waters and adapted from David Lebovitz. Makes a 9-inch round cake INGREDIENTS: For the topping: • 4 tablespoons unsalted butter • 3/4 cup light brown sugar, lightly packed • 1 pear, ripe but firm • 1/2 - 3/4 cup whole cranberries, fresh or frozen For the cake batter: • 1/2 cup unsalted butter, room temperature/squishy-soft • 3/4 cup granulated sugar • 2 large eggs, room temperature • 1 teaspoon vanilla extract • 1-1/2 cups all-purpose flour • 1-1/2 teaspoons baking powder • 1/4 teaspoon salt • 1/2 cup whole milk, room temperature INSTRUCTIONS: Position an oven rack to the lower third of the oven and preheat the oven to 350°. Lightly butter the sides of a 9-inch round cake pan and dust with flour. Line the bottom with parchment paper. For the topping: Melt the butter and brown sugar in a medium saucepan over medium heat, stirring frequently until the mixture begins to bubble. Remove from heat and cool. Meanwhile cut the pear in half lengthwise and remove the core. Slice further into quarter-inch wedges. Arrange the pears and cranberries in a single layer in the bottom of the cake pan, atop the parchment paper. Pour the melted butter-sugar mix over the fruit and spread it out evenly. Use a small offset spatula or your fingers to spread, especially if the mixture has firmed up. Set aside. For the cake: In a small bowl combine the flour, baking powder and salt. In a 3-quart mixing bowl, use an electric mixer on medium-high speed to beat the 1/ 2 cup of softened butter and granulated sugar until very light and fluffy, about 3 – 5 minutes. Scrape the sides of the bowl frequently. Reduce the electric mixer to medium speed and add the eggs, one at a time, mixing well between each addition. Add the vanilla extract and continue mixing until blended. On low speed add half of the flour mixture, then the milk and finally the rest of the flour mixture. Take care to avoid over mixing. You can finish the mixing by hand with a spatula to make sure the flour is barely incorporated into the batter. Spread the batter evenly over the fruit. Bake for about 45 minutes. Test for doneness with a toothpick inserted into the center of the cake. It should come out clean, with maybe a crumb or two clinging on. Remove from the oven and cool on a wire rack for 10 minutes. Run a small knife around the edge of the pan. Place the serving plate over the cake pan and quickly flip it over so the bottom of the cake and all the caramelized fruit is on top. Note: Test the heat of the cake pan before picking it up and inverting it onto the serving place. If too hot for comfort, use a kitchen towel or potholders to protect your hands. Serve warm. Makes a 9-inch round cake INGREDIENTS: For the topping: • 4 tablespoons unsalted butter • 3/4 cup light brown sugar, lightly packed • 1 pear, ripe but firm • 1/2 - 3/4 cup whole cranberries, fresh or frozen For the cake batter: • 1/2 cup unsalted butter, room temperature/squishy-soft • 3/4 cup granulated sugar • 2 large eggs, room temperature • 1 teaspoon vanilla extract • 1-1/2 cups all-purpose flour • 1-1/2 teaspoons baking powder • 1/4 teaspoon salt • 1/2 cup whole milk, room temperature INSTRUCTIONS: Position an oven rack to the lower third of the oven and preheat the oven to 350°. Lightly butter the sides of a 9-inch round cake pan and dust with flour. Line the bottom with parchment paper. For the topping: Melt the butter and brown sugar in a medium saucepan over medium heat, stirring frequently until the mixture begins to bubble. Remove from heat and cool. Meanwhile cut the pear in half lengthwise and remove the core. Slice further into quarter-inch wedges. Arrange the pears and cranberries in a single layer in the bottom of the cake pan, atop the parchment paper. Pour the melted butter-sugar mix over the fruit and spread it out evenly. Use a small offset spatula or your fingers to spread, especially if the mixture has firmed up. Set aside. For the cake: In a small bowl combine the flour, baking powder and salt. In a 3-quart mixing bowl, use an electric mixer on medium-high speed to beat the 1/ 2 cup of softened butter and granulated sugar until very light and fluffy, about 3 – 5 minutes. Scrape the sides of the bowl frequently. Reduce the electric mixer to medium speed and add the eggs, one at a time, mixing well between each addition. Add the vanilla extract and continue mixing until blended. On low speed add half of the flour mixture, then the milk and finally the rest of the flour mixture. Take care to avoid over mixing. You can finish the mixing by hand with a spatula to make sure the flour is barely incorporated into the batter. Spread the batter evenly over the fruit. Bake for about 45 minutes. Test for doneness with a toothpick inserted into the center of the cake. It should come out clean, with maybe a crumb or two clinging on. Remove from the oven and cool on a wire rack for 10 minutes. Run a small knife around the edge of the pan. Place the serving plate over the cake pan and quickly flip it over so the bottom of the cake and all the caramelized fruit is on top. Note: Test the heat of the cake pan before picking it up and inverting it onto the serving place. If too hot for comfort, use a kitchen towel or potholders to protect your hands. Serve warm. READ IT IN THE POST The Wine Corner All about Domaine Tour Boisee By Pierre du Mont It’s hard to imagine how much wine is made in the Languedoc region of France. Curving along the Mediterranean from Provence to close to the Spanish border it is a vast, wild area covered with grape vines that were first planted by the Romans two thousand years ago. It is often combined with Roussillon, its neighbor to the south. Together they have 700,000 acres of vines, the biggest vineyard area in the world - producing more wine than the entire U.S. For many years, the wines were churned out by co-operatives and the emphasis was more on quantity than quality. Any grocery store in France will feature hundreds of bottles of Languedoc wine starting at 2 euros. But the exciting story in Languedoc is the emergence over the past two decades of many artisan winemakers who care deeply about the quality of their wines and whose finest examples can compete with any wine region in France. It’s good news for the consumer because the reputation has not quite caught up with the wines; they still represent remarkable bargains selling in the U.S. for between $10 and $20. This month we will explore my very favorite Languedoc producer. (The best way to find these wines is to use the Wine Searcher app.) Domaine La Tour Boisee I have twice had the opportunity to visit this charming winery located in the small village of Laure Minervois. The property includes part of a medieval stone wall and tower that gives the winery its name. We were greeted by Jean-Louis Poudou. the owner, and Florence Hallett, the gracious business manager who walked us through the lineup of about 13 wines. Winery Owner Jean-Louis Poudou. The 2017 Marie-Claude Chateau Tour Boisee Minervois. The flagship wine is the 2017 Minervois Cuvee Marie-Claude an inky monster that has a rich blueberry nose that leaps from the glass. In the mouth it is rich and full bursting with blackberry fruit and finishing with firm tannins. I brought this wine to a blind tasting recently and it killed wines four times more costly. Available for less than 15 Euros. it is a remarkable value. Another killer wine from Tour Boisee is the 2018 Carignan from 60-year-old vines. It is rich, complex, dark and opulent. It oozes dark berry fruit and has a smooth, soft finish. This has become my house wine. Everyone I have poured it for has ended up buying a case. Amazingly it is available on the internet for around $10 a bottle. A value like this does my French/Scottish heart good. The winery has come out with a new label since I first visited. The 2019 Un Historie de Famille is a blend of Grenache, Domaine La Tour Boisee in the village of Laure Minervois, France. Syrah, Mourvedre and Carignan. It appears to be a sort of second label to the flagship Marie Claude and has similar aromas and tastes but is lighter in body and has a shorter finish. It is also an excellent value. Viognier is a notoriously temperamental wine to vintify, so I was delighted that the 2019 Viognier Bel Serrat came out so well. It is medium bodied with understated floral aromas, plus notes of white pepper, green apple and lime. Zesty on the palate, it picks up vibrant citrus notes on the brisk finish. Drink over the next few years. The 2019 Malbec/Alicante Bel Serrat is the lightest of Tour Boisee’s red wines. I have never seen these two grapes blended together but this combination of 80% Malbec and 20% Alicante Bouchet works quite well. It smells of cherries and plums and is light and supple in the mouth with a clean finish. This is a perfect picnic wine to accompany charcuterie and cheese. Saving the best for last I have saved my favorite for last – a wine that is history in a bottle. In 1905 a farmer in Miniervois Laure planted a vineyard with 23 different varietals of grapes. (Reading the list of the varietals on the info sheet I confess to not having heard of half of them.) Vineyard blends often give great complexity to a wine. The 2018 Plantation 1905 is a vineyard blend on steroids. It as a beautiful nose of blackberries and black currants followed by a complex palate of plums, cherries and a touch of earth and leather. It gains complexity as it sits in the glass and ends with a smooth satisfying finish. Can’t think of a better companion to roast duck or cassoulet. Brilliant. The Plantation 1905 from Boisee.

articles.text: One of the rewards of sitting at a table outside the Piedmont Avenue Library is seeing the variety of patrons and hearing, if you ask, their stories. Sometimes you might even learn something. For instance, Michael, who lives across the street and subscribes to the HOOT, the library’s newsletter, uses a number of the library’s services. He checks out books, but he also receives them on his I-pad. He gets some books on Libby and others on Hoopla, both library programs. He streams movies and can access older media. He says that in non-COVID times the staff librarians are helpful and knowledgeable and he thinks the current team, brought together from several branches, is doing a remarkable job during this difficult time. Cora, who walked over, makes her requests online and picks up the books when she gets a notice they’re on site. Her children, six and four, really miss being able to go inside to attend Storytime, and miss being able to browse through the books. Debora, a regular patron, joined us and couldn’t give enough praises about the regular staff and the current service. “They deserve five stars….no, at least seven. It’s amazing how they’re coping,” she said. In the midst of patrons coming and going, collecting and returning books, a van with the library logo on its side pulled up in the loading zone on the street. Todd, the driver, unloaded several bins full of books onto a dolly and pushed them to the back door of the library. Soon he returned with a bigger load of books from inside the library, hauled them to the van, then headed to the main library. Three of these vans and drivers provide this service to all the branches in the city. Sumona, with a tiny baby strapped to her chest, and a four-year-old at home, has been coming to the library for four years, She likes books on Kindle; and her husband prefers hard copy books. Keeping library services available for readers and listeners is a real challenge these days, but five days a week, from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m., Emily Odia and her crew are there, making sure patrons get the books they ordered. articles.text: The Cancer League’s 47th annual Holly Ball event will be held this Friday evening, December 4, but without the traditional dinner event at the Claremont Country Club. Jenna Caldwell, this year’s Holly Ball Chair, was committed to continuing The Cancer League’s fundraising tradition, but safely. She and her committee came up with something that would look a little different. “So many people are avoiding their doctor’s offices and are putting off the early detection screenings, making them even more at risk. While the world has changed, our commitment to fighting cancer can’t,’ she said. This year’s theme is: Don’t Stop the Fight Against Cancer, Holly Ball 2020 virtual. The virtual event kicks off on Friday, December 4 at 7:00 p.m. with welcoming comments from Cancer League President Lucy Ridgway, followed by featured speakers Alan Ashworth, PhD, President of UCSF Helen Diller Family Comprehensive Cancer Center, and Dr. Mekhail Anwar, recipient of the NIH New Innovator Award and recipient of seed funding from The Cancer League. Additionally, Hanna Malak, a member of the Board of Directors at Camp Okizu, will describe the work done by Okizu, a camp helping children affected by cancer to heal through a welcoming recreational outdoor camp program. Sadly, the camp recently sustained significant damage from the North Complex fires. To maintain as much tradition as possible, the Holly Ball organizers teamed up with the Claremont Country Club to offer wonderful meals and signature cocktails to go prepared by the Club’s Executive Chef, Hans Wiegand. The Cancer League welcomes all guests to join this special event. To make a donation of any level and to purchase to-go meals, see thecancerleagueinc. org/hb2020.

articles.text: Pete LaChapelle, a former resident of Piedmont, died on November 3, 2020. He was 84. Born Peter Hall LaChapelle in Detroit, Michigan on February 23, 1936, he grew up in Webster Groves, Missouri and Denver, Colorado. He attended East High School in Denver and played on the school basketball and baseball teams. He played two years on the All-State basketball team and was inducted into the East High School Sports Hall of Fame. He attended Stanford University where played on both the basketball and baseball teams for the Indians. He joined the Beta Theta Pi fraternity and graduated with a B.A. in Economics. Pete went on to earn a law degree at Lincoln Law School in San Jose and spent a 30-year career working as a Deputy District Attorney for the Alameda County Counsel’s office. His true joy was spent on the baseball field as a coach. He coached a variety of teams of all ages for over 45 years, including Hyatt House in the Young America League in Oakland, the Highlanders in the Piedmont Pony league, and for many years as assistant coach for the Piedmont High School baseball team. Hundreds of kids knew him as Coach LaChapelle, the guy that remembered their birthdays, what position they played, their batting average or ERA, and usually a career highlight or two. After retiring from the County Counsel’s office, he continued to coach at Piedmont High, helping to mentor new generations of players. He loved watching the San Francisco Giants and was in attendance for some of the team’s most memorable moments: opening day at Candlestick Park, the last game played at Candlestick, Pete LaChapelle, Piedmont High School’s former assistant baseball coach for many years, died on November 3. He was 84. Barry Bonds’ record setting home run, opening day at Pac Bell Park, and the winning 2014 World Series game at AT&T park between the Giants and the KC Royals. He was an avid runner, running every day around Lake Merritt or on the trails in the Oakland hills. Pete spent a lifetime loving music. Whether singing at a party, playing his ukulele, harmonizing with friends and family, music was a constant source of joy. What started out as an opportunity to join the Kingston Trio became a personal hobby shared with family and friends over a lifetime. Pete was known for his dry wit and fantastic sense of humor. Never without a quick comeback, or a great practical joke, Pete always loved a good one-liner. Pete is survived by his loving wife of 43 years, Barbara LaChapelle, son Steve of Oakland; daughter Tracy, her life partner Sid Wagner, and her son, Michael Hageman of Cobb, Californial; son Tom, wife Alex and their daughters, Sadie and Josie of San Luis Obispo; and son Erik, wife, Mayra and their son, Oliver, of Alcala de Henares, Madrid, Spain. He is also survived by step-daughter Suzanne Heske and sons Alden, Benjamin, and Owen of Piedmont, and step-son Jeffrey Cathrall, wife Brenda and son Jake, of Rock Tavern, NY. There will be a private celebration of life with family. McBain said that the city’s ability to attract and retain high-quality professionals makes working in Piedmont city government an incredibly positive experience. “I’ve always made a big effort to listen to city staff as a whole. We’ve been fortunate over the years to have people who are very talented and honest,” he said. “There’s a tremendous amount of information, intelligence, and experience in this staff, and you have to take advantage of that, and I think I’ve tried to do that.” McBain has been active as a volunteer in Piedmont for 16 years. He served on the Recreation Commission for six years and was its Chair for two years. He also served on the Municipal Tax Review Committee in 2011, one year before his election to City Council. Indoor dining is prohibited. Retailers can operate only at 25 percent capacity. Indoor museums, fitness centers and religious services must close. On November 19, the state announced that Purple Tier counties must follow a “stay at home” order prohibiting non-essential work, movement and gatherings between 10 p.m. and 5 a.m. The order is currently scheduled to end 5 a.m. on Monday, December 21, although it may be extended or revised. The new order allows restaurants to operate after 10 p.m. for takeout. People are free to go to the grocery store or pharmacy. People can also walk their dog in their neighborhood. The county is urging the public to stay home, wear face masks and maintain social distancing protocols. The surge in Alameda County echoes a general uptick throughout the United States. Health officials nationwide have warned about potential spikes in COVID-19 due to Thanksgiving and other upcoming holidays. The vast majority of counties in California are in the Purple Tier. As of press time, the California Department of Public Health reported that there have been 1,225,189 cases of COVID- 19 in California. Cases have trended upward since October 18 in the state. There have been 19,211 deaths due to the disease statewide. Bob McBain and his wife Pam held a modest election night event at his house for volunteers who helped in his re-election campaign in 2016. In addition to his years in elected office, McBain served as the Investment Chair for the Piedmont Educational Foundation, a past board member of the Piedmont Parents’ Club, and a deacon and leader at Piedmont Community Church, in addition to being a trip leader for three years on the church’s mission service project in Mexico during Spring Break. McBain will be succeeded by Vice Mayor King. “Working with Bob has been a dream,” King said. “Always the consummate professional, Bob shows nothing but respect, calm and humor as he tackles the significant issues facing our city. I’ve learned so much from him,” she said. Former City Administrator Paul Benoit, who worked with McBain throughout his five-year career in Piedmont, offered similar sentiments. “Over my 35 plus years in City government I have worked with well over a hundred different council members and many different mayors. Bob ranks among the very best – and in both categories. He has a special talent for focusing in on what matters most, and was always a calm and steadying influence - especially when a difficult issue had potential get heated and out-of-hand,” Benoit said. “Those qualities were bolstered by his intelligence and keen wit. As mayor, Bob was always supportive. He was someone I regularly turned to for sage advice – and when I needed a hearty laugh. Bob was among a number of Piedmonters who made my time with the City a highlight of my career.” Benoit’s successor, current City Administrator Sara Lillevand, said that she has benefited greatly from McBain’s guidance. “Bob took his job as Mayor quite seriously, but never took himself too seriously,” she said. “Bob is comfortable, confident and patient enough to let good ideas emerge through listening and dialogue without ever needing credit – even though he often has the good idea first. His leadership skills are outstanding and have particularly shined during COVID,” she said. Although McBain’s volunteer years in Piedmont have come to a close, there is still work to do over the next few years concerning the rebuilding of the Piedmont Community Pool. McBain has no obligation to continue working on plans for the facility, but said that he will be available when needed. “It’s going to be a wonderful project for the city to work forward to. I’m confident it will attract interest, funding, and donations to make it a really beautiful facility,” he said. It was unusual for the city to place a bond on the ballot. Measure UU, the bond that will generate funding to build a new pool, was the first public bond the city has ever put forward. “It was a great team that [councilmember] Betsy Andersen put together. Her Sovereign Majesty Queen Elizabeth II will resume monarchical duties over all states, commonwealths, and territories (except Arkansas, which she does not fancy). A questionnaire may be circulated next year to determine whether any of you noticed. To aid in the transition to a British Crown Dependency, the following rules are introduced with immediate effect: You should look up “revocation” in the Oxford English Dictionary. 1. Then look up aluminium and check the pronunciation guide. You will be amazed at just how wrongly you have been pronouncing it. 2. The letter ‘U’ will be reinstated in words such as ‘favour’ and ‘neighbour.’ Likewise, you will learn to spell ‘doughnut’ without skipping half the letters, and the suffix -ize will be replaced by the suffix -ise. Generally, you will be expected to raise your vocabulary to acceptable levels. (look up ‘vocabulary’). 3. Using the same 27 words interspersed with filler noises such as “like” and “you know” is an unacceptable and inefficient form of communication. There is no such thing as US English. We will let Microsoft know on your behalf. The Microsoft spell- checker will be adjusted to take account of the reinstated letter ‘u’ and the elimination of -ize. You will relearn your original national anthem, God Save The Queen. 4. July 4th will no longer be celebrated as a holiday. 5. You will learn to resolve personal issues without using guns, lawyers, or therapists. The fact that you need so many lawyers and therapists shows that you’re not adult enough to be independent. All American cars are hereby banned. They are crap and this is for your own good. When we show you German cars, you will understand what we mean. 8. All intersections will be replaced with roundabouts, and you will start driving on the left with immediate effect. An internal revenue agent (i.e. tax collector) from Her Majesty’s Government will be with you shortly to ensure the acquisition of all monies due (backdated to 1776). 17. Daily Tea Time begins promptly at 4 pm with proper cups, never mugs, with high quality biscuits (cookies) and cakes; strawberries in season. articles.text: Dress Best for Less, the nonprofit retail store that contributes money to Piedmont schools, generated $3,466 in sales during its annual one-day Ski Sale, The event usually draws a larger number of buyers, but the absence of snow in the mountains and the impact of coronavirus combined to limit sales to about one-half of normal. Despite this, Dress Best for Less Vice President Linda Smith Munyan said that they were satisfied with the total, given the overall plunge in retail sales nationwide due to COVID-19. “People had to wait in line to get in,” she added. There were many logistical changes made this year in order to comply with public health regulations. In prior years Dress Best for Less accepted cash only during its one-day ski sale. This year, they made the change to contactless payment after discussing their plans with the City of Piedmont. “We submitted a full-site plan to the city and event layout and traffic flow that had to be approved before we could proceed with the sale,” Smith Munyan said. Other changes in 2020 included common sanitary fixtures seen in most retail establishments during the COVID-19 pandemic. Staff had to limit the number of people allowed inside, and masks were required. One entry and a separate exit point was made to allow for easy social distancing, and a plexiglass shield was installed at the cash register. DBFL still has lots of great ski and snowboarding gear available for sale at its retail store on Piedmont Avenue next to Piedmont Grocery. You can still donate new and gently used ski and snowboarding gear, but donations are made by appointment on Tuesdays, Wednesdays and Saturdays. Schedule a time by clicking on: https://bit.ly/DBFL-Donations. Photos by Julie Reichle A long line of people waited to purchase items at the annual Dress Best for Less Ski Sale on November 15. A plexiglass shield was installed at the cash register as a health precaution.
